titleEn: I love that the LORD hears my voice
progression: | Em Em | Am Em | C D | Em Em |
intro: Nineteen verses of one person's thanksgiving after a near death, and one of the six psalms of Hallel (113 to 118), said on festivals, on Rosh Chodesh, and at the seder, where the second part of Hallel comes after the meal. Two things to watch. The psalm keeps returning to one refrain, calling on the name of the LORD, at verses 4, 13 and 17, and it uses that refrain to turn a rescue into an obligation. And the grammar is unusual in places: second person feminine endings in -chi where standard Hebrew has -ch, and a suffix on {{12.4}} that looks Aramaic, which is part of why the date of the psalm is argued over.

stichs.en: I love, because the LORD hears my voice,
my pleas for mercy.

verses.summary: The psalm opens with a verb and no object. What is loved is left unsaid until the next clause supplies a reason, which is exactly why translators disagree about whether the object is God or the fact of being heard.

stichs.en: Because He turned His ear down to me,
I will call out all my days.

verses.summary: The reason is physical: an ear tilted down toward someone lower. What follows is a commitment covering a whole lifetime, made on the strength of one answered call.

stichs.en: The cords of death wound around me,
the narrow places of Sheol found me;
trouble and sorrow I found.

verses.summary: Death is drawn as rope and as narrow ground, two images of being squeezed. The last clause flips the grammar: the straits found him, and then he found trouble.

stichs.en: And I called on the name of the LORD:
please, LORD, save my life.

verses.summary: The hinge of the first half. It is also the first of three places where the psalm says the same thing about calling on the name, and the only one where the call is made from inside the danger.

stichs.en: Gracious is the LORD, and just,
and our God shows mercy.

verses.summary: One rescue is generalised into a statement about character, and the pronoun goes plural: our God, not mine. Nothing in this verse is about the speaker.

stichs.en: The LORD guards the simple;
I was brought low, and He saved me.

verses.summary: A claim about who gets protected: not the strong or the clever but the ones with no defences. The speaker then quietly files himself under that heading.

stichs.en: Return, my soul, to your rest,
for the LORD has dealt well with you.

verses.summary: The speaker turns and addresses his own soul in the feminine, the way one addresses a person, and tells her to go back to a rest she already had before the trouble started.

stichs.en: For You rescued my life from death,
my eye from tears,
my foot from stumbling.

verses.summary: Three rescues in one verse, running down the scale from the whole life to the eye to the foot, from the fatal to the merely ordinary.

stichs.en: I will walk before the LORD
in the lands of the living.

verses.summary: The result of the three rescues, and the only future the first half asks for. Not triumph, only going on walking where the living walk.

stichs.en: I kept faith even when I said,
I am greatly afflicted.

verses.summary: The second half opens by looking back at the worst moment and insisting that the trust and the complaint were happening at the same time, not one after the other.

stichs.en: I said in my panic,
every person is false.

verses.summary: The verdict pronounced in panic is quoted and left standing, not corrected. The psalm is willing to let its speaker be wrong out loud.

stichs.en: What can I give back to the LORD
for all His dealings toward me?

verses.summary: The question that organises everything after it. The three answers that follow are a cup, a vow and a sacrifice, and all three are performed in front of other people.

stichs.en: I will lift the cup of deliverance
and call on the name of the LORD.

verses.summary: The first answer, and the strange one: it involves receiving rather than giving. Lifting a cup counts here as repayment, and the plural noun keeps the rescues countable.

stichs.en: My vows to the LORD I will pay,
in front of all His people now.

verses.summary: The second answer. What was promised in private distress is settled in front of witnesses, and the witnesses are what make it a payment rather than a feeling.

stichs.en: Precious in the eyes of the LORD
is the death of His faithful ones.

verses.summary: The hardest verse in the psalm and the reason it is read at funerals. Whether precious here means valued or means costly, and so not lightly allowed, is disputed.

stichs.en: Please, LORD, I am Your servant,
I am Your servant, son of Your maidservant;
You have loosed my bonds.

verses.summary: The speaker states his legal status twice, adds his mother to establish that he was born into the household rather than sold into it, and ends with the vocabulary of freeing a slave.

stichs.en: To You I will offer a thanksgiving sacrifice
and call on the name of the LORD.

verses.summary: The third answer, and the only one that costs an animal. The refrain about calling on the name comes back for the last time, now attached to an offering instead of to a cry for help.

stichs.en: My vows to the LORD I will pay,
in front of all His people now.

verses.summary: The vow line repeats word for word. The repetition is not filler: this time a location follows in the next verse, so the promise finally gets an address.

stichs.en: in the courts of the house of the LORD,
in your midst, Jerusalem.
Halleluyah.

verses.summary: The psalm ends where the payment happens, in a courtyard in a named city, and the last two words are a plural imperative that hands the praise over to everyone else.

pardes.body: Two halves with a seam at verse 10. Verses 1 to 9 tell what happened: cords, straits, a call, a rescue, and a modest future in which the speaker simply keeps walking. Verses 10 to 19 ask what is owed and pay it. Verse 12 is the pivot question and verses 13, 14 and 17 are its three answers, a lifted cup, a vow settled in public, and a thanksgiving offering. The refrain about calling on the name of the LORD ties the halves together: it is a cry for help at verse 4 and a liturgical act at verses 13 and 17, the same words doing opposite work. Note also that the psalm never says what the danger was. It gives the shape of the trouble ({{3.0}} surrounded, {{3.1}} cords) and never the cause, which is part of why anyone can say it.

This is a psalm of strange forms. {{7.2}} and {{7.6}} carry a second person feminine ending in -chi where standard biblical Hebrew has -ch, and the same ending shows up on {{19.3}}; {{12.4}} takes a suffix of the type ordinarily found in Aramaic. These are usually read as marks of a late composition, though the dating is disputed and an archaic-dialect explanation has also been proposed. Verse 10 is the famous crux: the particle {{10.1}} can be read as because, or that, or concessively as even when, and the Greek translation took it in the sense of therefore, giving I believed, therefore I spoke, which is a different sentence altogether. One more seam worth knowing: the Greek and Latin traditions split this psalm in two at verse 10, which is why the numbering of the psalms differs between Jewish and some Christian bibles through this stretch of the book.

Two readings that the text invites without needing a source attached. First, {{15.0}}, precious: if the word means valued, the verse consoles, and if it means costly, it says that God does not spend the lives of the faithful cheaply, which is why the same verse can be read as comfort at a funeral and as an argument for staying alive. The two readings are both current and the choice between them is disputed. Second, {{16.10}}, my bonds, together with the double declaration of servanthood: a slave born in the household could not simply walk away, so the psalm has the speaker claim the status and then thank God for undoing the restraint that came with it. Being God's servant is presented as the freedom, not as the chain. And because verse 13 is said with a cup in hand at the seder, the lifted cup of the psalm and the cup on the table are heard as one act, whatever the derivation.

In the mystical reading the psalm is addressed inward. {{7.0}} tells the soul to return, using the verb of repentance, and the rest it is sent back to is not a place the soul reaches but a state it originally had. The soul is spoken to in the feminine throughout, as the receiving side of the relation, and the cup of {{13.0}} is the standard image for that side: a vessel whose whole worth is its capacity to be filled and then lifted. Read this way the answer to the question of verse 12 is deliberately paradoxical. What one gives back to the giver of everything is the act of receiving properly and in public, which is why {{6.5}} saves and {{9.0}} walk are not two different endings but the same one, an ordinary life continued on borrowed time.
